strengths: Novel contrastive guidance framework (Eq. 5) combining repulsion from memorized content with attraction toward a high-quality alternative is elegant and well-motivated

Insightful empirical analysis in Section 5.1 revealing fundamental differences between verbatim and template memorization in cross-attention patterns, motivating dynamic per-prompt detection over fixed rules

Comprehensive and methodologically sound experimental evaluation across two SD versions and two memorization types, with honest filtering to high-SSCD cases and extensive ablations on blocks, heads, timesteps, and alternative components
Consistent state-of-the-art performance across all settings (Table 1) where prior methods excel in different subsets, demonstrating superior robustness
Strong empirical results showing large improvements over prior CA-based methods (e.g., SSCD 0.517 vs 0.602 for Ren et al. on template memorization)
Practical inference-time approach requiring no retraining, aligning with realistic deployment scenarios where practitioners use pretrained models
Robustness validation on non-memorized prompts (Section A.3) showing the method doesn't degrade quality when memorization is absent
Clear presentation with excellent appendix including implementation details, hyperparameter ranges, and detailed ablations supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited architectural scope—only evaluated on Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v2.0; generalization to SDXL, Flux, or other T2I models remains unclear, reducing confidence in robustness across future architectures

Fundamental practical limitation requiring prior knowledge of which prompts are memorized at inference time to apply mitigation; while non-memorized robustness is shown, identifying memorization a priori is often the actual challenge

Spike detection mechanism uses simple Z-score thresholding with threshold τ that varies significantly across settings (Table 2), but no principled strategy for selecting τ is provided beyond empirical tuning
Repulsion term r in GUARD framework is motivated only intuitively as alleviating quality degradation pressure; the mechanism is not rigorously analyzed or justified theoretically
Hyperparameter selection requires different ranges for different settings (Table 2), suggesting sensitivity that may not transfer to new models/datasets without extensive retuning
Significant computational overhead—3 forward passes per timestep results in ~1.45x wall-clock slowdown compared to baseline (Table 5), which is non-negligible for deployment at scale

Some design choices appear arbitrary: 15% quality degradation threshold for hyperparameter selection, choice of Z-score threshold at 3, different acceptable CLIP scores for different memorization types (0.254 vs 0.186)
SSCD metric limitations not discussed—measures pixel/feature similarity but may not fully capture memorization; conversely, similar images could arise coincidentally
Incremental novelty over prior work—builds on Ren et al. (2024)'s cross-attention approach, adding dynamic detection and contrastive guidance, but core techniques are established
Missing deeper analysis: no visual examples showing success/failure cases, no investigation of when the method struggles, limited explanation of why template memorization is structurally harder

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem of memorization in T2I diffusion models with a pragmatic inference-time approach
Novel empirical analysis (Figure 1) revealing different CA patterns for verbatim vs. template memorization, motivating dynamic detection over fixed strategies
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple settings with careful ablations on blocks, heads, and timesteps
Demonstrates robustness on non-memorized prompts (Section A.3), important for practical deployment
Consistent empirical improvements over baselines (Ren et al. 2024, Wen et al. 2024, Han et al. 2025) across both memorization types
Clear presentation and well-motivated problem formulation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution reduces to Z-score outlier detection + logit attenuation + guidance wrapping, which is straightforward engineering rather than novel methodology
Small dataset sizes (72-143 prompts) with wide confidence intervals and no statistical significance testing, raising concerns about generalizability of claims

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: paper shows dynamic detection beats fixed detection empirically but doesn't explain why instance-specific triggers matter or how repulsion/attraction terms interact
Hyperparameter sensitivity across settings (τ ranges from 0.01-0.05 to 1.5-3.0 in Table 2) with method-specific tuning that could bias comparisons
Filtering to SSCD > 0.7 evaluates only highly-memorized examples; generalization to mildly memorized cases (more prevalent in practice) unclear
Missing key ablations: no direct comparison of repulsion-only (r=0) vs. attraction-only (s=0) components to isolate GUARD's benefits
Limited generalization: evaluated only on Stable Diffusion v1.4/v2.0; architecture generalization (DALL-E, Flux, etc.) and language generalization not addressed
Incomplete analysis of template memorization: all methods degrade substantially compared to verbatim, but mechanistic explanation for this fundamental challenge is lacking
Practical deployment questions unaddressed: how practitioners identify which prompts are memorized, whether universal application helps defensively, threat models undefined
Insufficient comparison to recent concurrent work (Han et al. 2025); choice of Z-score over other outlier detection methods not justified

strengths: Exceptional empirical analysis (Figure 1) revealing that memorization-critical tokens extend beyond EOT and differ between verbatim/template memorization, directly motivating the dynamic approach and explaining prior method failures

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation across three settings with thoughtful experimental design (SSCD > 0.7 filtering, Pareto frontier analysis, extensive ablations on blocks/heads/timesteps, robustness testing on non-memorized prompts)
Consistent and substantial improvements across all settings, particularly impressive for template memorization on SD v2.0 (SSCD: 0.19 vs 0.36 for prior SOTA)
Practical inference-time method that requires no retraining, works universally without knowing memorized prompts, uses efficient batching for minimal overhead
Honest and transparent treatment of limitations (white-box threat model constraints, inference-time fundamental limitations, proxy metrics for quality)
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, well-structured exposition, insightful figures, and comprehensive appendix enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification for key design choices: Z-score outlier detection not compared against alternatives (modified Z-score, isolation forests), multiplicative attention scaling not motivated against alternatives
Architecture generalization concerns: only evaluated on Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v2.0; no experiments on other major T2I models (DALL-E 3, Imagen, Flux) limits generalizability claims

Hyperparameter sensitivity and complexity: three hyperparameters with architecture-specific ranges (τ varies from [0.01, 0.05] to [0.5, 3.0]), unclear principled selection strategy for practitioners without access to memorized prompts
Quality metrics are proxies with limitations: CLIP has known semantic alignment issues, FID computed on unrepresentative distribution; no human evaluation studies on image quality or naturalness
Limited evaluation dataset: 500 initial memorized prompts, filtered to 72-143 per setting; relatively small and single-source (Webster 2023) - would benefit from larger/multi-source dataset
Incomplete ablations: no isolated ablation of repulsive-only term (r > 0, ϵ+ = ϵ∅), limited exploration of alternative positive targets beyond CA and semantic paraphrasing

Incomplete technical analysis: continuous spike recomputation cost at every denoising step under-analyzed, performance degradation with lower SSCD thresholds unexplored, interaction with guidance scale parameter (s) not examined

strengths: Valuable empirical analysis revealing different cross-attention patterns for verbatim vs template memorization, providing insights that explain failures of prior hard-coded approaches
Principled dynamic spike detection using per-prompt statistical outlier analysis, avoiding fixed token-based strategies that fail across memorization types

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple architectures (SD v1.4, v2.0, v3.0), memorization types, metrics (SSCD, CLIP, FID, DINO), and extensive ablations with rigorous statistical reporting
Consistent empirical improvements over prior work, with particularly strong gains on challenging template memorization (SSCD 0.193 vs 0.356 for Ren et al. on SD v2.0)
Practical efficiency achieving near-single-forward-pass execution through intelligent batching with modest memory overhead
Robustness to non-memorized inputs (Section A.3) suggests universal applicability without prior memorization detection
Honest treatment of limitations including white-box vulnerability, inability to remove weights, and architecture-specificity concerns
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: GUARD framework is straightforward extension of classifier-free guidance (Eq. 5); primarily an engineering contribution combining known concepts rather than introducing fundamentally new algorithms

Architecture-dependent design: entire approach depends on U-Net structure; unclear generalization to transformer-based models (SD v3.0 evaluation limited to only 39 examples with SSCD > 0.3) and other T2I systems

Spike detection lacks theoretical grounding: Z-score threshold τ is ad-hoc without principled justification; empirically requires wide ranges across settings ([0.01, 0.05] to [0.5, 3.0]); sensitivity analysis of τ is limited
Requires setting-specific hyperparameter tuning (τ, α, r with different ranges per architecture-memorization type), limiting practical deployment compared to hyperparameter-free approaches

Missing mechanistic understanding: paper doesn't explain why CA attenuation prevents memorization; connection between attention spikes and memorization is correlational rather than causal with no causal validation

Evaluation protocol filtering to SSCD > 0.7 excludes mildly memorized examples that are easier to mitigate; criticism of Han et al. (2025) for different protocols seems unfair as complementary approaches serve different purposes
Template memorization remains substantially challenging even with CA-in-GUARD (SSCD 0.517 vs 0.079 for verbatim on SD v1.4), suggesting unaddressed fundamental limitations
Non-trivial quality degradation in some settings (e.g., SD v1.4 template: CLIP 0.219→0.186); practical deployment would require separate memorization detector to avoid applying mitigation universally

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem of memorization in text-to-image diffusion models with practical inference-time approach

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple architectures (SD v1.4, v2.0, v3.0), memorization types (verbatim/template), metrics (SSCD/CLIP/FID/DINO), and robustness checks (samplers, steps, guidance scales)
Valuable empirical insight that template vs verbatim memorization exhibit different cross-attention patterns, revealing limitations of prior methods (Ren et al. 2024) that only attenuate EOT tokens
Methodologically rigorous with proper statistical reporting (confidence intervals), extensive ablations in appendix, filtering justification, and robustness evaluation on non-memorized prompts
Honest discussion of limitations acknowledging that inference-time methods don't erase weights and cannot defend against white-box attacks
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the GUARD framework (Eq. 5) is a straightforward modification of classifier-free guidance adding a single term. The claimed framework contribution is overstated given tight coupling to the specific CA attenuation instantiation

Spike detection mechanism using z-score-based outlier detection is standard statistical technique, not particularly novel or sophisticated. Hyperparameters (τ, α) appear somewhat arbitrary and lack principled selection

Heavy dependence on prior work (Ren et al. 2024) for CA attenuation mechanism. Main improvements appear to come from better per-prompt spike detection rather than GUARD framework itself, as evidenced by strong performance of CA attenuation alone (r=0 case)

Evaluation protocol differs from prior work (filtering SSCD > 0.7, separate verbatim/template results). While justified, this complicates fair comparison. Traditional protocol results relegated to appendix show closer performance to baselines

Limited practical applicability: requires architecture and memorization-type-specific hyperparameter tuning (e.g., τ ranges 0.01-0.05 for verbatim vs 0.5-3.0 for template). Method cannot be applied universally without knowing memorization type a priori

No theoretical analysis explaining why this approach works or justifying design choices (multiplicative scaling, specific U-Net blocks, threshold values). Limited conceptual insight into memorization mechanisms

Small high-memorization sample sizes (72-143 prompts) make results potentially noisy. SD v3.0 evaluation limited to only 39/500 prompts, with authors acknowledging memorization may differ in transformer-based models

Relatively simple contributions presented as framework: primarily combines existing CA attenuation from Ren et al. with standard guidance modification and z-score outlier detection. Each component individually is straightforward

strengths: Strong empirical analysis of cross-attention patterns across memorization types with clear insights (Figure 1), revealing that template vs verbatim memorization require different mitigation strategies
Novel GUARD framework combining repulsion and attraction terms with principled contrastive guidance, properly motivating each component
Dynamic per-prompt spike detection via Z-score thresholding outperforms prior hard-coded approaches (CA attenuation achieves SSCD 0.19 vs 0.36 for Ren et al. on SD v2.0 template)
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple architectures (SD v1.4, v2.0, v3.0), memorization types (verbatim and template), and metrics (SSCD, CLIP, FID, DINO) with extensive ablations
Practical efficiency maintained at inference-time with minimal computational overhead while achieving consistent improvements; method shown robust to non-memorized prompts (Table 3)
Principled hyperparameter selection protocol with clear justification; honest treatment of limitations and differences from prior evaluation protocols; ~1,500 GPU hours demonstrates rigor
Well-structured presentation with clear motivation; valuable finding that template memorization is harder to mitigate than verbatim, providing important insights for future work
weaknesses: Hyperparameter threshold τ shows extreme sensitivity across settings (0.01-3.0 in Table 2); no principled a priori selection method provided, limiting practical deployment guidance

Evaluation protocol departures from prior work (SSCD > 0.7 filtering) makes direct comparison difficult; while justified and full-spectrum results provided in appendix, main claims could be better caveated about this difference

Limited mechanistic understanding of why template memorization proves harder; Figure 7 analysis relegated to appendix; aggregation strategy (max attention over spatial queries) lacks justification versus mean/median alternatives
Some performance improvements modest with overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., CLIP scores in Table 1); statistical significance testing absent; FID reported without confidence intervals
Relatively small dataset (72-143 highly memorized examples per setting; only 39 for SD v3.0), limiting generalizability; no evaluation on newer memorization benchmarks
Han et al. (2025) outperforms on SD v1.4 template memorization (SSCD 0.479 vs 0.517), contradicting claims of consistent dominance; failure modes and underperformance cases not discussed
Crucial implementation details (batched forward pass handling of spike detection across three simultaneous streams) scattered between main text and appendix, potentially impacting reproducibility
Inference-time only approach doesn't address underlying memorization in weights; requires knowing which prompts are memorized; white-box threat model remains unaddressed despite practical importance
